nameStory: Carolina redroot gets its name from its striking red roots and underground stems (rhizomes) that look like they're stained with blood when you dig them up. The "Carolina" part reflects where botanists first described this wetland beauty, though it actually ranges much further north into New England. Some folks also call it bloodroot, but don't confuse it with the spring wildflower of the same name!
description: Carolina redroot is a wetland perennial that looks like a small, delicate grass or iris at first glance. It grows in clumps with narrow, sword-like leaves that can reach 1-3 feet tall. In mid to late summer, it produces clusters of small, pale yellow flowers on slender stems. What makes this plant truly special is hidden underground - those famous bright red roots that give it its name.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Six pale yellow petals (technically tepals) form small, star-shaped flowers about half an inch across, clustered at the top of thin stems in mid to late summer

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Bright red to orange-red roots and rhizomes that stain your hands when handled - this is the plant's signature feature and most reliable identifier

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy, growing in clumps from the base with parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small colonies in wet areas, with individual plants 1-3 feet tall growing from underground rhizomes

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in wet, acidic places - if the ground isn't soggy and the soil isn't sandy or peaty, you're probably looking at something else

habitat: Carolina redroot loves wet feet and acidic conditions, making its home in cranberry bogs, swamps, pond edges, and wet sandy areas throughout New England's lowlands. You'll often find it growing alongside sphagnum moss, pitcher plants, and other bog specialists in places where the soil stays consistently moist. It's particularly fond of sandy, peaty soils that most other plants would find too acidic and waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green from the soggy ground, looking like small clumps of grass or young iris plants.
seasonality.summer: Pale yellow flowers bloom from mid to late summer on slender stalks above the foliage - this is prime identification time.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, and flowers give way to small seed capsules.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely above ground, but those red roots and rhizomes persist underground, ready for spring.

funFact: Carolina redroot is considered such a troublesome weed in commercial cranberry bogs that growers have developed special management strategies just for this one plant - its red roots spread underground and can quickly take over sections of valuable cranberry beds!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse this with the spring wildflower bloodroot (Sanguinaria canadensis) - that one has white flowers, broad lobed leaves, and blooms in early spring in forests, not summer in wetlands. If you see grass-like leaves and wet ground, you're probably looking at Carolina redroot.
contextualKnowledge: The name "bloodroot" causes confusion because there's a completely different plant (Sanguinaria canadensis) with the same common name. That bloodroot is a spring woodland wildflower with white flowers and broad leaves, while Carolina redroot is a summer-blooming wetland plant with yellow flowers and narrow leaves. Both have reddish roots that "bleed" when cut, hence the shared name.
compareHints: Carolina redroot is the only species in its genus Lachnanthes, making it unique in New England. Within its family (Haemodoraceae), it's most similar to some iris family plants, but those typically have showier flowers and different growth patterns. The combination of wet habitat, grass-like leaves, small yellow six-petaled flowers, and especially those bright red roots make it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
